narration: The most famous photo of this fish shows a body that had already collapsed.

heading: Cold open
narration: Blobfish look weird because nearly every picture you have seen shows one out of the water, after a trawl from the deep, its soft body slumped and damaged.

heading: Cold open
narration: In deep water the same animal is held in shape. NOAA's rule for seawater puts the pressure at 1000 metres at roughly 101 atmospheres, and a body built for that does not keep its form on a ship's deck.

heading: Cold open
narration: The pink, drooping face with the nose-like flap is real in the sense that a camera recorded it.

heading: Cold open
narration: It is not what the animal looks like where it lives. So the interesting part is not that the fish looks strange.

heading: Cold open
narration: It is how anyone knows what it really looks like, when almost nobody has seen one alive.

narration: Why do blobfish look weird?

heading: The famous face is a collapse, not a design
narration: Start with what the animal is. The name blobfish usually refers to Psychrolutes marcidus, a fathead sculpin that lives in deep water off southeastern Australia and New Zealand.

heading: The famous face is a collapse, not a design
narration: Sculpins are a large group of mostly bottom-living fish, and many of them have broad heads, wide mouths and tapering bodies.

heading: The famous face is a collapse, not a design
narration: Nothing about that outline is strange. If you drew an ordinary sculpin and then softened its edges, you would be close to what this fish looks like at home.

heading: The famous face is a collapse, not a design
narration: The face in the famous photo is something else. The nose-like flap is not a nose.

excludes: the living shape of the fish

heading: The famous face is a collapse, not a design
narration: It is loose skin and soft tissue from the head, sagging forward and down because nothing is holding it up.

heading: The famous face is a collapse, not a design
narration: The downturned mouth is the same tissue pulled by gravity. The pink, glossy surface is partly the result of skin being scraped away in a net.

excludes: the living shape of the fish

heading: The famous face is a collapse, not a design
narration: So the blobfish face only exists in air. It is the shape a living body takes once it has lost the medium that was supporting it, which means the photo shows a body slumped in air, not the living shape of the fish.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: To see why, think about density. The flesh of this fish is close to the density of seawater.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: In the sea, that matters enormously. The water carries the weight of the body, so the tissue does not need much internal structure to keep its shape.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: Lift the same fish into the air, and air carries almost none of that weight.

stages: flesh close to the density of seawater

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: All of the soft tissue now hangs from whatever skeleton and muscle lies underneath, and in this fish there is not much of either.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: So gravity pulls soft tissue down, and the animal spreads out like something set down on a table.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: You have probably seen a gentler version of this yourself. A jellyfish in the sea is a bell with a clear shape.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: The same jellyfish on a beach is a puddle. Nothing about its anatomy changed between the two.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: The only thing that changed is what was supporting it. A blobfish is not as watery as a jellyfish, but the principle is the same, and it explains most of the strangeness in a single step.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: Depth adds a second factor. NOAA explains the rule that governs it: for every ten metres you descend in seawater, pressure rises by roughly one atmosphere.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: At the surface you are already under one atmosphere from the air above you.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: At 1000 metres the water adds about a hundred more, for a total of roughly 101 atmospheres.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: Blobfish have been caught from depths in this general range, though the published figures vary between sources.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: Deep-living animals are built for that load. Their tissues are mostly water, and water barely compresses, so the pressure itself does not crush them.

heading: Water holds up a body that air cannot
narration: The trouble comes when the pressure is taken away quickly, during a haul to the surface the body was never built to survive.

heading: Producer POV
narration: Trees look passive and are constantly responding, communicating, reallocating, surviving across timescales we barely register.

args.text: Trees look passive and are constantly responding, communicating, reallocating, surviving across timescales we barely register.

heading: A fish that looks inert is doing careful work
narration: A blobfish has the same problem as anything people call passive. Resting on or just above the seafloor, it can look as if it is doing nothing at all.

heading: A fish that looks inert is doing careful work
narration: In fact its whole body is an answer to a hard question: how to stay at a chosen height in the water, in the cold and the dark, while spending as little energy as possible. The softness you laugh at in the photo is the answer.

heading: Gelatinous flesh is a solution, not a defect
narration: Many fish control their depth with a swim bladder, a gas-filled organ they can inflate or deflate.

heading: Gelatinous flesh is a solution, not a defect
narration: Gas is costly to manage at depth, because the deeper you go, the more it is squeezed, and the more work it takes to keep that bladder filled.

heading: Gelatinous flesh is a solution, not a defect
narration: Like many deep-water fish, the blobfish does not rely on a gas-filled swim bladder.

heading: Gelatinous flesh is a solution, not a defect
narration: Instead, its buoyancy comes largely from its body. Its gelatinous flesh is slightly less dense than the water around it, so the fish can hover just above the seafloor without constantly swimming.

heading: Gelatinous flesh is a solution, not a defect
narration: Picture a large head, loose skin over soft tissue, and a tapering tail. That is the working animal.

heading: Gelatinous flesh is a solution, not a defect
narration: There is a trade in this design. The fish gets buoyancy without a gas-filled swim bladder, and very little energy spent holding position.

narration: What it gives up is muscle, and with it the strength for fast swimming.

heading: Gelatinous flesh is a solution, not a defect
narration: That suits an animal thought to wait near the bottom and take small animals that pass close to its mouth.

heading: Gelatinous flesh is a solution, not a defect
narration: The setting explains why saving energy matters so much. The Smithsonian's ocean pages describe the deep sea as cold, dark and short of food, with much of what is eaten down there sinking from the waters above.

heading: Gelatinous flesh is a solution, not a defect
narration: In a place like that, an animal that burns little energy just to stay where it is has an advantage.

heading: Gelatinous flesh is a solution, not a defect
narration: A firm, muscular body would be stronger. It would also be more expensive to run.

heading: Pressure is the second injury, and the net is the third
narration: Now follow a specimen up. Blobfish are usually brought up as bycatch in deep-water trawls, nets dragged near the bottom for other species.

heading: Pressure is the second injury, and the net is the third
narration: First comes time in a net among other animals and debris. Then comes scraping that strips skin, because the skin is thin and loose and tears easily.

heading: Pressure is the second injury, and the net is the third
narration: Then comes a rapid drop in pressure and rise in temperature, as the net climbs through water that is warmer and far less pressurised than home.

args.title: What a trawl haul does

a rapid drop in pressure and rise in temperature

heading: Pressure is the second injury, and the net is the third
narration: By the time it reaches the deck, the body arrives already damaged.

heading: Pressure is the second injury, and the net is the third
narration: It is worth being careful about which injury does what. Popular explanations sometimes say the fish explodes or melts on the way up.

includes: damage from pressure falling too fast
excludes: the main cause of the slump

heading: Pressure is the second injury, and the net is the third
narration: That overstates it. Decompression is damage from pressure falling too fast, and it can harm tissue, especially in animals that carry gas inside them.

heading: Pressure is the second injury, and the net is the third
narration: But for a soft, low-muscle fish without a gas-filled swim bladder, decompression is likely not the main cause of the slump.

includes: damage from pressure falling too fast
excludes: the main cause of the slump

heading: Pressure is the second injury, and the net is the third
narration: The larger factor is the loss of support from water, made worse by skin damage from the net. Air and gravity do most of the reshaping.

narration: So how does anyone know what a blobfish looks like alive? Mostly by taking cameras down to the animal instead of bringing the animal up.

heading: Living images tell a different story
narration: Images of living blobfish and their close relatives do exist, and they show what the physics predicts: a pale, pinkish fish with a large head, a recognisable mouth, fins, and a body that holds its outline.

heading: Living images tell a different story
narration: It looks soft, and a little loose around the edges, but it looks like a fish.

heading: Living images tell a different story
narration: Set the trawled photo beside one of those images and you are looking at the same kind of animal in two states, one supported and one not.

heading: Ugly is a statement about where we stand
narration: This is why the blobfish became famous for the wrong reason. A photograph of a trawled specimen spread widely online, and the fish was later voted the world's ugliest animal in a public poll.

heading: Ugly is a statement about where we stand
narration: The vote was light-hearted, and it drew attention to deep-sea animals that rarely get any.

heading: Ugly is a statement about where we stand
narration: But it was judging a damaged body in air. It was a little like judging a jellyfish by the puddle on the beach.

heading: Ugly is a statement about where we stand
narration: There is a broader lesson for how you read any deep-sea image.

heading: Ugly is a statement about where we stand
narration: Almost every animal in the deep is adapted to conditions you never experience: cold, darkness, little food, and pressure many times what you feel at the surface.

heading: Ugly is a statement about where we stand
narration: Photograph one on a ship's deck and you are photographing it outside every one of those conditions at once.

heading: Ugly is a statement about where we stand
narration: The picture is accurate about the specimen and misleading about the species.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: When the two images sit side by side, look at the head first.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: In the trawled photo, the head has no edge; it pours forward over the mouth.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: In the living image, the head has a boundary, and the mouth sits where a fish's mouth should.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: Then look at the skin. Where it is glossy and raw, the net has been at work.

heading: What to notice in the edit
narration: The trawled photo is a record of the specimen, honest about what happened to one fish. It is not a portrait of the species.

heading: Closing
narration: The face that made this fish famous is the face of a fish that has left its world.

heading: Closing
narration: Down where it lives, held in cold water under great pressure, it is simply a soft fish doing a quiet, efficient job. The strangeness was in where we stood to look.
